entry.title: Counting days is not measuring phase

link.title: Counting days is not measuring phase

entry.content:
Most datasets and studies that work with the menstrual cycle assign phase by counting days from the last period. The count is a proxy for an underlying hormonal state, and a weak one. In 1,498 cycles from 157 women tracked with a urinary-hormone monitor, a fixed calendar rule placed a session in its intended cycle phase 53 to 60 percent of the time, depending on the window. The physiology these labels stand in for varies across the cycle, so a label that is wrong a third to a half of the time is not a small measurement detail… It sets a ceiling on what any downstream analysis or model can recover.

Importance of the phase label

Women are half the population, however the datasets behind health AI and motion science were built almost entirely on male or sex neutral physiology (Jiang et al., The Lancet Digital Health). Where the cycle is considered at all, it enters as an estimated independent variable: a session is labelled follicular or luteal, and outcomes are compared across those labels.

Hormonal state across the cycle is associated with measurable shifts in neuromuscular function, strength, sleep and cognition. A meta-analysis of 22 studies reported moderate shifts in maximal muscle strength favouring the late follicular phase (Niering et al., 2024), and grip and isokinetic torque vary across biochemically confirmed phases in physically active women (Weidauer et al., 2020)… can you imagine how sports performance are impacted over this changes?

The difficulty is that the label is usually estimated, not measured. Calendar counting and basal body temperature stand in for hormonal confirmation, and each introduces error at the exact point where the signal is read. Models trained on data labelled this way inherit the error, and biomedical AI systems already underperform for women when trained on non-representative data (Cirillo et al., 2020; Joshi, 2024). Before asking whether a cycle effect exists, it is worth asking how often the label naming the phase is correct.

Research Question AND experiments

The Marquette Menstrual Cycle Data contains day by day records from women using an electronic fertility monitor that reads urinary luteinizing hormone and an estrogen metabolite (Fehring, 2012; Fehring et al., 2013). The monitor marks a hormonally defined peak day near ovulation, which gives a per-cycle anchor that calendar counting does not.

I used the monitor tracked cycles, 1,498 cycles from 157 women, and took the peak day as the ovulation reference. The question is simple: without the monitor, assigning phase by counting days instead, how often would you be right?

Findings

  1. Ovulation does not normally happen on day 14 Ovulation fell on a median of day 15, with an interquartile range of day 14 to 18. It landed exactly on day 14, the textbook value, in 15 percent of cycles. Luteal length was also variable, with a median of 13 days and an interquartile range of 12 to 14.

A woman’s own history helps, but only partly. The within woman standard deviation of the ovulation day was 2.2 days, and the intraclass correlation was 0.64. About a third of the variance in ovulation timing sits within women across their own cycles, so a personalized estimate built from a woman’s average still leaves a two day spread around any single cycle. The day-14 assumption is wrong for most cycles, and one woman’s mean does not determine the current mean.

  1. A day-21 visit is not the luteal phase Scheduling makes the cost concrete. The table below shows how often three common rules place a session in its intended window, across the same 1,498 cycles.
Target window Fixed calendar day Backward from usual length Backward from actual length
Mid-luteal (ovulation +5 to +9) 60% 66% 77%
Periovulatory (ovulation -2 to +1) 53% 57% 73%

Next, two things: A fixed day visit misses its intended phase in a quarter to nearly half of cases, and the direction of counting matters. Counting backward from the realized length of the cycle, when it is known, is consistently better than counting forward from the last period, because luteal length is more stable than follicular length.

  1. There is a statistical cost Phase misclassification does not only mislabel cases, it attenuates the effect under study. When a fraction of sessions carry the wrong phase, a real difference between phases is diluted toward zero, and more participants are needed to recover the same power. Under a simplified all or none misclassification model, the inflation in required sample size ranged from about 1.7 for actual length backward counting to 2.8 for the fixed day-21 rule. These figures are an approximation, not a precise correction.

What is not in doubt, though, is the direction. A single session per woman, scheduled by calendar, detects only large effects, and part of the inconsistency in the cycle literature is likely noise in the phase label rather than the absence of an effect. In programs designed specifically for women, sessions scheduled according to a hormonal marker, such as an LH urine test, eliminate most of this disadvantage.

Interpretation and suggestions

Although the monitor gives a hormonally defined peak day, it is a urinary marker rather than serum, so it bounds how well calendar counting could do rather than defining ground the truth exactly. The cohort is also women with regular cycles tracking to conceive, so the spread in the wider population, including adolescence and the perimenopausal transition, is likely wider, not narrower. The analysis is exploratory and the sample size figures are illustrative.

The practical implications for experiments design are specific:

  • Confirm phase with a hormonal marker wherever the design allows it.
  • Where it does not, count backward from the realised cycle length rather than forward from the last period, and do not treat day 14 and day 21 as fixed.
  • Report the phase assignment method explicitly. An effect measured against confirmed phase and one measured against a calendar label are not the same measurement.

For anyone building cycle aware wearables or models, the label is the FOUNDATION!!!!. If it is wrong a third of the time, everything trained on it inherits that error. Counting days is cheap… It is also wrong often enough to matter.

Data, code and references

The analysis and notebooks are in the public repository Hormones-Brain-Motion. The source is the Marquette Menstrual Cycle Data.

entry.title: What resting EEG can and cannot say about the menstrual cycle

link.title: What resting EEG can and cannot say about the menstrual cycle

entry.content:
This public EEG dataset let us ask a direct question: do resting brain rhythms differ between women on hormonal contraception and naturally cycling women, or across the menstrual cycle? With 37 contraceptive users and 32 non-users, the answer this dataset can support is that it cannot tell. After correction for multiple comparisons, no spectral measure differed between groups. This does not prove that cycling does not alter the resting EEG. The dataset is too small to detect anything more than a significant effect, and the method used is too imprecise to determine the phase.

The Experiment

ds007615 (Normannseth et al., 2025) contains resting state EEG from 69 women, 37 using hormonal contraception and 32 naturally cycling. I compared seven standard spectral measures between the two groups, including absolute and relative alpha power and the individual alpha peak frequency, and corrected for the seven tests with the Holm procedure.

The Findings

No measure differed between groups after correction. The largest raw effect was absolute alpha power, with a standardized difference of d = 0.48, but its 95% confidence interval ran from −0.00 to 0.96: consistent with a moderate effect and equally consistent with none. Relative alpha power (d = 0.33) and individual alpha peak frequency (d = −0.36) were smaller and also non significant.

The useful question is not whether the test was significant, but what it could have found. The minimum detectable effect for the contraceptive contrast was 0.69 SD. For a luteal vrs other comparison within the naturally cycling women, it was 1.13 SD. Lesser effects than that were never within reach. Detecting a moderate between groups effect (d = 0.5) at conventional power would need roughly 64 women per group, about twice this dataset.

A design for woman measurements, changes the arithmetic. Measuring the same women at two cycle points, rather than comparing different women once, would bring the minimum detectable effect down to about 0.35 SD with 27 women, assuming a within subject correlation of 0.8. The gain comes from removing between person variation, which in resting EEG is large.

The phase labels are also crude: The phase labels in a dataset like this are assigned by counting days, not by measuring hormones. Here the cycle is divided into fixed day ranges (1–6, 7–12, 14+), and a binary follicular/luteal split places the ovulatory window into the luteal class. Recomputing the label by counting backward from each woman’s cycle length changes it for 14 of 26 cycles. A comparison built on these labels is comparing noisy groups, which widens the confidence intervals further. It is the same calendar problem that undermines day-based phase assignment elsewhere, now sitting on top of an already underpowered test.

My suggestion on experimental design

The honest reading of ds007615 is that it does not answer the question, and it says why: too few women, measured once, labelled by calendar. A dataset that could answer it would measure the same women across the cycle, with phase confirmed by a hormonal marker rather than a date. That is a different experimental design, not a larger version of this one.

Data, code and references

The analysis and notebooks are in the public repository Hormones-Brain-Motion.

  1. Pritschet L, et al. NeuroImage. 2020.
  2. Normannseth, et al. Frontiers in Human Neuroscience. 2025.
  3. OpenNeuro dataset ds007615. https://doi.org/10.18112/openneuro.ds007615.v1.0.0
entry.summary: A public EEG dataset of 69 women cannot separate a cycle or contraceptive effect from noise. A power and labeling analysis.

entry.title: Does a wrist-activity model underperform for women?

link.title: Does a wrist-activity model underperform for women?

entry.content:
A common argument for building female specific health data is that models trained mostly on men underperform for women. But I am a scientist so, for me it is worth testing directly rather than assuming. Using two public datasets, a wrist activity recognition benchmark and a national accelerometer survey, I looked for a sex or hormonal status effect on what the model learns and on the measured activity itself. At the resolution at which these datasets operate, the effect is so small as to be negligible. This does not invalidate the argument, but simply indicates where it applies.

##The Experiment

CAPTURE-24 (Chan et al., 2024) pairs wrist accelerometer data with camera confirmed activity labels for 151 adults, 99 women and 52 men. I trained a gradient-boosted classifier on 32 standard features to predict four coarse activity classes, and matched the training sets on age across 50 resamples so that sex, not age, drove any difference.

Macro F1 sat at 0.67 to 0.68 in all results. Training a model on a woman’s own sex rather than on a mixed set raised her macro F1 by 0.004 (95% CI −0.003 to 0.011). For men the gain was essentially zero. Between person variation minimized both, with a standard deviation of 0.088 across individuals. Of ten per-class comparisons, exactly one had a confidence interval excluding zero: light activity was classified better for women, by 0.015 F1. In the recognition of wrist activity at a general level, a trained model without regard to sex does not show significantly lower performance in the case of women.

In NHANES 2013–14 (3,815 adults with valid wrist accelerometry), women averaged 0.80 thousand MIMS per day more activity than men after age adjustment, so sex does move the aggregate. Hormonal status within women did not. Comparing menopausal and still menstruating women aged 40 to 59, the activity difference was d = −0.07 (95% CI −0.46 to 0.32), indistinguishable from zero. Across 679 menstruating women whose measured estradiol spanned a 25-fold range, there was no association between estradiol and daily activity (d = 0.03 per doubling, CI −0.03 to 0.09). NHANES carries no cycle day information, so this speaks to hormonal status and level, not to within cycle timing.

So… where is the Data Gap?

These are null results, and it is worth stating them clearly rather than trying to justify them. At the resolution of four activity classes and daily activity volume, neither sex nor hormonal status changes the model or the measure enough to matter. However, the claim that models underperform for women is not wrong in general. It needs to be made where it counts: fine-grained tasks, specific physiological signals, and outcomes known to track hormones, rather than coarse activity summaries with 4 class classifications…

The same logic applies to collecting new data. A dataset that can show a cycle effect has to resolve the cycle, with confirmed phase and repeated measures, which is exactly what population accelerometry and day labelled benchmarks lack.

My conclusion on these

Coarse wrist activity is close to sex neutral and hormone neutral in these datasets. It is the wrong place to look for the gender data gap, and a weak place to argue it from. The gap is real where the resolution is fine enough to see it. If you happen to know any dataset I could test this, please contact me :D

Data, code and references

The analysis and notebooks are in the public repository Hormones-Brain-Motion.

  1. Cirillo D, et al. npj Digital Medicine. 2020.
  2. Joshi A. Frontiers in Big Data. 2024.
  3. Chan et al. Scientific Data. 2024. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-024-03960-3
  4. NHANES 2013–2014, National Center for Health Statistics. https://wwwn.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes/
entry.summary: Testing the gender data gap on two public datasets. At coarse activity resolution, sex and hormonal status barely move the model or the measure.

entry.title: What is the data gap? The numbers behind it

link.title: What is the data gap? The numbers behind it

entry.content:
Women are half the population and a minority of the evidence. That is the data gap: the measurements, studies and datasets that medicine and health technology are built on describe male bodies better than female ones, and they almost never record the hormonal state that makes female physiology change over time. This post is the entry point to this blog. It sets out the gap in numbers. The other posts test pieces of it on public data.

How the gap was built

The gap has a documented origin. In 1977 an FDA guideline excluded most women of childbearing potential from early-phase drug trials. It stood until 1993, when the FDA rescinded it and the NIH Revitalization Act made the inclusion of women in federally funded clinical research a legal requirement (Liu and Dipietro Mager, 2016). Sixteen years of drug development ran under that exclusion, and many drugs prescribed today were approved before it ended (Zucker and Prendergast, 2020).

The rule is gone. Its effect on the evidence base is not, because data collected without women cannot be corrected afterwards. It can only be replaced.

How large it is today

Four audits, in four fields, counted the same thing in different ways.

Field What was counted Result
Open biosignal data 175 human datasets on PhysioNet Fewer than 7% report sex or gender, age, race and ethnicity together. Where sex is reported, samples are mostly male (Jiang et al., 2024)
Sport and exercise science 5,261 studies in six journals, 2014 to 2020 6% studied women only, against 31% men only. Women were 34% of 12.5 million participants (Cowley et al., 2021)
Neuroimaging Studies published since the 1990s Fewer than 0.5% consider health factors specific to women (Taylor et al., 2021; Jacobs, 2023)
Basic biology 720 articles in nine disciplines, 2009 against 2019 More studies include both sexes. In eight of nine disciplines, no more of them analyse by sex (Woitowich et al., 2020)

The first row is the one closest to my own work. PhysioNet is one of the largest open repositories of biosignal data, and it is widely used to develop, train and validate algorithms. An algorithm trained on a dataset that does not say who was measured cannot be checked for whom it works.

The last row is the most uncomfortable. Inclusion went up and analysis did not. Including women in a study and learning something about women are different things.

The variable that is never recorded

Sex is the easy part of the gap. A dataset can add a column for it. The harder part is that female physiology is not constant, and the variable that tracks the change is rarely measured.

Across one menstrual cycle, estradiol rises about 12-fold and progesterone about 800-fold (Pritschet et al., 2020). A woman goes through roughly 450 cycles in her lifetime (Rizor et al., 2024). More than 100 million women use oral hormonal contraceptives, which suppress the body’s own hormone production and replace that rhythm with a different one (Taylor et al., 2021).

These swings reach the signals that wearables already collect. In 274 cycles from 91 women wearing a wrist sensor during sleep, pulse rate was 2.1 beats per minute higher in the fertile window than during menstruation, and 3.8 beats per minute higher in the mid-luteal phase (Shilaih et al., 2017). Body temperature rises by 0.28 to 0.56 °C after ovulation, and in a cohort of 237 women, wrist skin temperature, heart rate and respiratory rate all shifted with cycle phase (Goodale et al., 2019).

A device that does not know the cycle phase has to attribute those shifts to something else: fitness, recovery, stress, illness. The measurement is correct. The interpretation is missing a variable. How well that variable can be recovered without a hormone measurement is a separate question, and I test it in another post.

What the gap costs

Three population-scale numbers show where it lands.

Drugs. Women experience adverse drug reactions nearly twice as often as men (Zucker and Prendergast, 2020). Most pharmacotherapeutic guidelines remain sex-neutral, although absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion all differ by sex and vary with hormonal state (Aljohmani and Yildiz, 2025).

Diagnosis. In hospital records from 6.9 million people, the whole Danish population over 21 years, women were diagnosed later than men for 770 disease types, by about four years on average (Westergaard et al., 2019). A registry records the age at first diagnosis, so it cannot by itself separate later onset from later recognition. Either way, the pattern holds across hundreds of conditions.

Autoimmune disease. In records from 22 million people in the UK, 19 autoimmune disorders together affect about 10% of the population: 13% of women and 7% of men (Conrad et al., 2023). A disease group that affects women at nearly twice the rate of men depends on the same evidence base described above.

What is not settled

None of this means every reported cycle effect is real. Whether athletic performance changes with cycle phase is still called “a constant scientific debate”, made harder by studies that never measured the hormones (Schlie et al., 2025). For pain, most well-controlled studies in healthy women find no effect of phase (Iacovides et al., 2015).

I take that uncertainty seriously, and I think it has the same cause as everything above. Small samples, single sessions and unmeasured hormones produce inconsistent results in both directions. A field cannot settle a question with data that was never collected to answer it.

Why this is personal

I do not come to this topic only as an engineer. I live with an autoimmune disease, and I am tracking my own body recomposition. When I look at my own numbers, I want to know which changes are the ones I am working for and which belong to my cycle or to my condition. That question is the data gap at the scale of one person, and it is the reason I keep working on it.

Where to go next

Each post on this blog takes one public dataset and one question.

  • Counting days is not measuring phase: how often a calendar date identifies the cycle phase, tested on 1,498 hormone-tracked cycles.
  • What resting EEG can and cannot say about the menstrual cycle: what a public EEG dataset of 69 women has the statistical power to detect.
  • Does a wrist-activity model underperform for women?: whether sex or hormonal status changes an activity model and a national accelerometer survey.
